text.p: Sweden's AB Volvo and Japan's Mitsubishi Motors Corp on Wednesday announced closer cooperation at their joint venture Dutch car plant which analysts saw as a logical move that could lead to further ties.

Volvo Cars announced it was expanding its collaboration with Mitsubishi in technical development and production areas at the NedCar plant which is owned equally by the two companies and the Dutch government.
Analysts welcomed the closer links but saw the relationship remaining one of cooperation, with a focus on Volvo's engine strategy, and dismissed merger suggestions.
"I think it is a logical step and a natural evolution between the two," said UBS auto analyst Simon Miller.
"I'd expect cooperation to go further. They have a good relationship and the NedCar venture is steadily improving."

Volvo Cars said the two partners had agreed to consider more opportunities for cooperation including the development of engine component technology and the joint development of a future car platform to be produced at NedCar.
"The two companies will commence studies for the next generation of cars beginning production at the start of the 21st century," a statement from Volvo Cars said.
The Nedcar plant at Born produces Volvo's S40/V40 models and Mitsubishi's Charisma with production running at 200,000 cars a year in 1996.
The two companies have already said they would consider exploring a form of cooperation in the truck sector.
"Perhaps that may well involve the development of a next generation of medium weight trucks," Miller said.
The two companies said they recently signed a contract for Mitsubishi to supply Volvo with its Gasoline Direct Injection (GDI) engine for Volvo's S40 and V40 models produced at NedCar.
The GDI engine offers low fuel use and high power output.
"The two companies are currently also considering the possibility of the incorporation of GDI technology within the Volvo engine family," Volvo said.

Analyst Hans Westerberg from Den Danske Bank said the extended cooperation would put a focus on Volvo's engine strategy as the company had concentrated on performance since it dropped plans to merger with Renault in 1994.
"Volvo is too small and hasn't had enough power to focus on performance and fuel efficiency and Mitsubishi will help them," Westerberg said.
Auto analyst Francois Colli from Paribas said the extended collaboration was no surprise.
"It is good for Volvo that they have this cooperation because they're a small player. Mitsubishi is a small player in Europe too although it is big elsewhere," Colli said.
"There is a natural gain in doing this. I think they will collaborate further but I don't think they want to merge. They are happy with this relationship."

Last December Volvo and Mitsubishi said they would consider jointly selling commercial vehicles in Europe, sharing car components globally, while Volvo's truck unit would supply heavy trucks to Mitsubishi's sales network in Asia.
